parole.testo: Blend of: * Inherited from Proto-Slavic *valъ (“surge, wave”). * Resultant noun of валя́ (valjá, “to tumble, to plummet”), iterative verb from *valъ. * Instrumental noun of ва́лям (váljam, “to roll”), causative/inchoative verb from *valъ. * Technical meaning borrowed from Russian вал (val), ultimate

Reflects Proto-Slavic *gybъkъ (“flexible”), possibly borrowed from Russian ги́бкий (gíbkij). Cognate with Macedonian гибок (gibok) (dialectal). Morphologically identical to ги́бам (gíbam, “to flex, to hang, to thread”) (dialectal) + -ък (-ăk).

parole.significato: to disfigure, to deform, to uglify
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *groziti, а causative-iterative verb of obsolescent гроза́ (grozá, “menace”). The literary meaning is borrowed from Russian грози́ть (grozítʹ, “to threaten”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *grǫbъ /*grubъ via a Western dialect; possibly reinforced by Russian гру́бый (grúbyj).

Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *zveno, but the exact course of descent is disputed: * Borrowed from Russian звено́ (zvenó), at least for the standard meanings; * Possibly inherited, as evident by doublets such as dialectal звъна́ f (zvăná), дзво́но (dzvóno, “piece, bit, slip”).

parole.significato: to touch, to affect, to concern
parole.testo: Factitive-iterative of obsolete ко́сна (kósna, “to touch, to affect”). Diachronically, inherited from Proto-Slavic *kasati, with literary sense reinforced at a later time by Russian каса́ться (kasátʹsja).

parole.significato: to span, to wind, to unwrap
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *katati, with some meanings borrowed from Russian ката́ться (katátʹsja) (from the same origin).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krǫtъ, with some of the meanings influenced by Russian круто́й (krutój, “drastic”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *naborъ (equivalent to *na- + *borъ (“assembly”)). Meaning “cohort” is borrowed from Russian набо́р (nabór), from the same proto-Slavic word.

parole.significato: act of care, heed, concern (towards s.o.)
parole.testo: Formally, inherited from Proto-Slavic *něga. Poetic meanings are borrowed from Russian не́га (néga) (from the same origin).
From Proto-Slavic *paluba, probably via Russian па́луба (páluba). Morphologically formed as па- (pa-) + луб (lub, “plank, ledge”) (dialectal).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *prěmъ /*pramъ (cf. Serbo-Croatian пре̏ма /пра̏ма (“albeit, towards”)), reinforced at a later time by Russian прямо́й (prjamój) (from a regional variant *pręmъ).

parole.significato: to strike, to pound, to bash
parole.testo: Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *raziti. Literary sense is borrowed from Russian рази́ть (razítʹ).
O-grade deverbal of река (reka, “to say”). Diachronically, inherited from Proto-Slavic *rokъ. Poetic meaning is reinforced from Russian рок (rok, “fate”).
From Proto-Slavic *sъkatъ, probably via the intermediate Russian скат (skat).

Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *sobolъ, *sobolь, possibly via Russian со́боль (sóbolʹ, “sable”), as Russia was the main exporter of sable pelt during the Middle Ages. Originally may have referred to any “small mammal with hazel or fawn fur”, based on the apparent kinship to dialectal соболе́ц (soboléc

Perhaps a conflation of: * Proto-Slavic *stěgъ (“post”), whence Serbo-Croatian стије̑г (“flagpost”); * Russian стяг (stjag, “flag”) (earlier Old East Slavic стѧгъ (stęgŭ)), itself from Old Norse stǫng (whence Swedish stång, Danish stang, English stang). parole.significato: male rival, male contender, male competitor, male emulator
parole.testo: Ultimately derived from Proto-Slavic *sǫpьrьnikъ, spread via the literary language. Diachronically, possibly borrowed from Russian сопе́рник (sopérnik). Synchronically, an agent noun of obsolete съ́пря се (sắprja se, “to altercate”) + -ник (-nik).
